sections.figure_alt: A shaded disk centered at the origin. The axes are labeled x1 and x2.
sections.body_md:
A quadratic program stops at flat constraints. A quadratically constrained quadratic program allows the inequalities themselves to be quadratic, and it stays convex only when each of those inequalities cuts a convex set.

Write a constraint as \(g(x)\le 0\) with \(g\) quadratic. The set is convex when \(g\) is a convex function, which for a quadratic is the positive-semidefinite test on the Hessian of \(g\). A disk is the model case: a sum of squares has a positive-semidefinite Hessian, and the inside of the disk is convex. The outside of the same disk reverses the inequality and is not convex. A product constraint such as \(xy\le 1\) has an indefinite Hessian and fails the same test.

The objective is still a convex quadratic. Convexity of the whole program needs the objective and every inequality.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
A constraint \(\tfrac12 x^T P x+q^T x+r\le 0\) is a convex constraint when \(P\succeq 0\). The disk
\[
(x-c_1)^2+(y-c_2)^2\le \rho^2
\]
is the case \(P=2I\). If the unconstrained minimizer of a convex objective lies outside the disk, the constrained minimizer is on the boundary, and the optimal value is the squared distance from that unconstrained point to the disk. The gap is the distance to the center, minus the radius, when the point is outside.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Minimize \((x-10)^2\) subject to \((x-1)^2\le 9\). The constraint is the interval centered at 1 with radius 3, so the feasible set is \([-2,\ 4]\). The parabola opens upward around 10, which lies to the right of the interval. The best feasible point is the right endpoint \(x=4\). The value is
\[
(4-10)^2=36.
\]
The optimal value equals 36. The center \(x=1\) is feasible and scores \((1-10)^2=81\), which is worse. The unconstrained point \(x=10\) scores 0 and is not feasible, because \((10-1)^2=81>9\).

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.body_md:
A negative eigenvalue in a constraint Hessian is not a harmless curve. It makes the feasible set fail the chord test. The outside of a disk is the usual picture: two feasible points can have a midpoint that falls in the hole.

Squaring a norm inequality is legal only when the side you square is nonnegative. A constraint written as a square from the start is already a quadratic inequality. Do not treat it as affine.

The zero eigenvalue is still positive semidefinite. A slab between two parallel lines, the square of one affine function, is a convex constraint even though its Hessian is singular.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: A Euclidean ball is both a convex quadratic constraint and a second-order-cone constraint, because a norm bounded by a constant is an affine upper bound. The cone form also allows the upper bound to tilt, which a single squared inequality hides less clearly. The cone program is the next description of this same disk, and of the tilted versions of it.
